chapters.title: Chapter 5: Integrity Signals in Filings and Behaviour

lessons.title: Dilution Watch: Preferential Allotments, Warrants and ESOPs

body.text: Your share of a company can shrink without you selling a single share. Dilution is the quietest way value moves from minority shareholders to someone else.

children.text: Companies issue new shares for good reasons: funding a plant, cutting debt, bringing in a strategic partner, paying employees. Every issuance also splits the same profits among more shares. Whether that helps or hurts you depends on three things: who received the shares, at what price, and what the company did with the money. This lesson turns those three questions into checks you can run from public filings.

body.caption: How each route treats existing minority shareholders

cells: Rights issue
All existing shareholders, in proportion to holdings
Set by the company, usually at a discount
Fairest. You can subscribe and keep your stake, or sell your rights entitlement on the exchange
QIP
Qualified institutional buyers only
Floor based on a two-week volume weighted average price, with up to a 5% discount allowed by special resolution
Neutral to mildly dilutive; quick and usually near market price
Preferential allotment of shares
Named investors, often promoters or connected parties
Not below the higher of the 90 trading day and 10 trading day volume weighted average price
Depends entirely on who is allotted and what the money is used for
Preferential allotment of warrants
Named investors, often promoters
Same floor price, with 25% paid upfront and the balance within 18 months
Weakest for minorities: it is an 18-month option on your company at today's price
ESOPs
Employees and directors, but not promoters or independent directors
Exercise price set by the company, often at a discount
Fair if modest and performance-linked; expensive if the pool is large and repriced

body.text: Lock-in is the quickest read on intent. Shares allotted preferentially to promoters carry a longer lock-in than those allotted to others. When you see a preferential issue, check the allottee list and the lock-in period in the postal ballot notice: it tells you whether this is long-term capital or a short-term trade dressed up as an investment.

children.text: Warrants: A Free Option Written by You

A convertible warrant lets the holder pay 25% of the issue price now and decide, any time within 18 months, whether to pay the remaining 75% and take the shares. If the stock rises, they convert and capture the gain. If it falls, they walk away and lose only the 25% already paid. That is an option, and the company received a premium of just 25% of the strike price for writing it.
Take 1 crore warrants issued to the promoter at ₹200, the floor price. The promoter pays ₹50 crore upfront. Two outcomes:

body.text: The forfeited 25% is booked by the company as a capital reserve, so management can describe a lapsed warrant issue as money the company kept. Do not accept that framing. The company sold an 18-month option on its own equity far below what such an option is worth, and minority shareholders wrote it.

body.latex: Diluted EPS = PAT / (Existing Shares + New Shares + Outstanding Warrants + Vested Options)
body.caption: Dilution hurts only if the money raised earns less than the company already earns

children.text: A company earns ₹600 crore on 30 crore shares, so EPS is ₹20 and the stock trades at ₹200, a P/E of 10. It issues 3 crore new shares at ₹200 in a preferential allotment, raising ₹600 crore. Whether you are hurt depends entirely on what that ₹600 crore earns. At a 10% post-tax return it adds ₹60 crore, profit becomes ₹660 crore on 33 crore shares, and EPS stays at ₹20. At 5%, profit becomes ₹630 crore and EPS falls to ₹19.09.

body.title: Dilution or Not?
body.prompt: Using the same company, suppose the ₹600 crore raised sits in deposits earning 5% after tax, adding ₹30 crore to profit. What is EPS after the issue? Answer in rupees to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Profit becomes ₹600 + ₹30 = ₹630 crore, spread over 33 crore shares, so EPS is ₹19.09, down from ₹20. The break-even return here is the earnings yield the company already earns on its equity. Money raised at ₹200 a share must earn at least ₹20 per share, a 10% post-tax return, for existing shareholders to be no worse off.

children.text: Who Gains Control While You Are Diluted

In the same example, suppose the promoter held 13.5 crore of the 30 crore shares, a 45% stake, and the entire 3 crore share preferential allotment goes to the promoter. The promoter now holds 16.5 crore of 33 crore shares: exactly 50%. Preferential allotments approved by a special resolution can, subject to conditions, be exempt from the open offer that would normally be triggered. So the promoter moved from 45% to 50% at the floor price, without making an open offer to you at a control premium.
The Long View: When Profit Grows and EPS Does Not

Serial dilution is easy to miss because every individual issue is explained and approved. The damage only shows when you compare profit growth with per share growth over several years. Here is an illustrative company that issued shares three times in six years.

body.title: Profit vs EPS when shares keep rising (indexed, Year 1 = 100)

children.text: Profit rose 26.7% over six years. EPS ended exactly where it started, at ₹20. Every rupee of growth went to the new shareholders who funded it, not the ones who were already there. Management can honestly claim the company grew. As an owner, you did not.
ESOPs: Pay That Comes Out of Your Stake

Employee stock options are dilution used as compensation, and are governed by SEBI's share based employee benefits regulations. Promoters and independent directors cannot receive them, which is why ESOPs are mainly a question about professional management rather than promoter extraction. They need shareholder approval by special resolution, the cost is charged to the profit and loss account, and outstanding options appear in diluted EPS.

columns.label: Reasonable
points: Pool of a few percent of equity, spread across many employees
Vesting over three to five years, often with performance conditions
Exercise price at or near market price on the grant date
Annual ESOP cost small relative to profit and disclosed clearly
No repricing when the stock falls

columns.label: Expensive
points: Large pools, repeatedly topped up by fresh shareholder resolutions
Most grants concentrated in a handful of senior executives
Deep discount exercise prices with short vesting
ESOP cost large enough that the company highlights profit before ESOP cost
Options repriced or regranted after a fall in the share price

body.text: When a company reports 'EBITDA before ESOP cost' as its headline number, read both versions. Stock options are a real cost paid in your ownership rather than in cash, and a company that grows only when that cost is excluded is growing on your dilution.

body.title: The Warrant Rule
body.textWithBlank: A convertible warrant holder pays ___% of the issue price upfront and has 18 months to pay the rest, forfeiting the upfront amount if they do not convert.
body.explanation: The 25% upfront payment makes a warrant an 18-month call option on the company's shares at today's floor price. That is why warrant issues to promoters deserve much closer scrutiny than plain share allotments.

body.title: Which Issuance Should Worry You Most?
body.question: A small cap company needs ₹400 crore. Which route should worry a minority shareholder the most?
options: A rights issue at a 15% discount to market price, open to all shareholders and with entitlements tradable on NSE
A QIP to institutional investors at a 4% discount to the two-week average price, approved by special resolution
Warrants issued to the promoter group at the floor price, with 25% paid upfront, at a time when the stock is near a two-year low
A preferential allotment of shares to an unrelated strategic partner at a 6% premium to market, with an 18-month lock-in
body.explanation: Warrants to the promoter near a two-year low combine three problems: the strike is set at a depressed price, the promoter gets 18 months to decide with only 25% at risk, and the promoter can increase its stake cheaply without an open offer. A rights issue lets you participate, a QIP is near market price, and a strategic investor paying a premium with a lock-in is usually a vote of confidence.

body.title: The Allotment That Follows a Fall
body.scenario: A mid cap engineering company's stock has fallen 45% over nine months on weak orders. Promoter holding is 41%, of which 30% is pledged. The board now proposes a preferential issue to promoter group entities: 2 crore equity shares plus 2 crore convertible warrants, both at ₹150, the ICDR floor price, against 25 crore shares currently outstanding. The stated purpose is 'general corporate purposes and working capital'. The company has ₹900 crore of cash and investments on its balance sheet, and no announced capex plan. The notice says the issue is exempt from an open offer.
body.prompt: What is actually happening here, and how would you vote on the special resolution?
body.modelAnswer: Follow the arithmetic and the timing. If all shares and warrants are converted, the promoter group gains 4 crore shares on a base of 25 crore, taking holding from 41% to about 49%, at a price set by a nine-month decline. The warrants give the promoter 18 months to decide with only ₹75 crore at risk out of ₹300 crore. And the company does not appear to need the money: ₹900 crore of cash with no capex plan, and a purpose described only as general corporate purposes. Set against 30% pledged promoter holding, the likely motive is strengthening control cheaply after a fall, not funding the business. Vote against, and say why in writing to the company. You would view it differently if the proceeds were tied to a specific, disclosed project with return estimates, if the pricing were at a premium to market rather than the floor, if there were no warrant component, and if the company did not already have surplus cash. Also check the half-yearly related party filings afterwards to see whether the new money leaves as loans to group companies.

body.title: Run a Dilution Check on One Holding
steps: On screener.in, compare ten years of net profit growth with EPS growth; a gap means dilution has taken part of the growth
Check the share capital line in the balance sheet each year and identify every year the count jumped
For each jump, find the corporate announcement: rights issue, QIP, preferential allotment, warrant conversion, or ESOP allotment
For preferential issues, read the postal ballot notice for the allottee names, the price against the market price on that date, the lock-in, and the stated use of proceeds
Check for outstanding warrants and unexercised options, and express them as a percentage of current shares outstanding
Compare basic and diluted EPS in the results: a persistent gap tells you how much future dilution is already committed
Track the promoter's stake through each event, and note any increase achieved without an open offer

body.text: Regulatory thresholds and pricing formulas are summarised here as they stand and can change; confirm the current SEBI ICDR requirements before acting. The examples are illustrative. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: Dilution shrinks your ownership without you selling anything, so judge every issuance by who received the shares, at what price, and what the money earned
Rights issues are fairest because you can participate or sell your entitlement; preferential warrants to promoters are the weakest for minorities
Warrants are an 18-month option on your company for 25% upfront: the holder converts if the price rises and forfeits the small premium if it falls
Dilution hurts only when the money raised earns less than the company already earns; at ₹200 a share with ₹20 EPS, new money must earn about 10% after tax to break even
Preferential allotments can lift a promoter from 45% to 50% at the floor price without an open offer, so track control alongside EPS
ESOPs are compensation paid in your ownership; watch pool size, concentration, discounting, repricing, and any use of profit before ESOP cost as the headline
